# What do university students know about Artificial Intelligence? Development and validation of an AI literacy test 

### Marie Hornberger [\*, Arne Bewersdorff, Claudia Nerdel ](#computers-and-education-artificial-intelligence)

_Technical University of Munich, Munich, Germany_ 

ARTICLE INFO ABSTRACT 

_Keywords:_ Artificial Intelligence (AI) strongly influences our daily lives and work environments. To deal with the challenges AI literacy as well as to pick up on the opportunities associated with AI, university students need to acquire a basic un- AI education derstanding of AI (so-called AI literacy). To design effective study programs that foster AI competencies, it is Higher education 

necessary to assess the state of students’ AI literacy. While there already are some AI literacy tests available, 

Test development Artificial intelligence many instruments focus on specific AI courses, rely primarily on self-assessment, or do not provide detailed 

psychometric information. This study aims to develop and validate an AI literacy test and to provide initial insights into the current state of AI literacy among German university students. We present a validated multiple- choice test to assess AI literacy in higher education. The results suggest that there is a significant variance in AI literacy among students, with most showing a fundamental understanding of AI. AI literacy is higher among students with a technical study background or prior experience in AI. The results imply that there is a need for effective AI courses for a broader audience of students who use AI in their daily lives and will use AI tools in their future careers. Furthermore, educators should consider the variance of students’ prior knowledge when 

designing AI courses.

audience. In this study, we develop and validate a test to provide in- sights into the current state of AI literacy among German university students with different study backgrounds. 

_1.1._ _Defining AI literacy_ 

Several frameworks outlining AI competencies and learning goals for various target groups have been published recently (Long & Magerko, 2020; Michaeli et al., 2022; Ng et al., 2021; Touretzky et al., 2019). A review of AI literacy definitions relevant for higher education by Lau- pichler et al. (2022) shows that despite the novelty of the concept, there seems to be a common understanding of AI literacy across many of these definitions (Laupichler et al., 2022). Following analogous constructs such as scientific literacy (Laugksch, 2000) or media literacy (Potter, 2010), AI literacy aims to describe competencies needed for a basic understanding of AI (Long & Magerko, 2020; Ng et al., 2021). Long and Magerko (2020) define AI literacy as “a set of competencies that enables individuals to critically evaluate AI technologies; communicate and collaborate effectively with AI; and use AI as a tool online, at home, and in the workplace”. They conceptualize AI literacy as a set of 17 com- petencies they derived from various literature sources. These compe- tencies are then grouped according to five questions (What is AI? What can AI do? How does AI work? How should AI be used? and How do people perceive AI?). By aligning with a widely used definition of AI literacy, our AI literacy test will be applicable for a wide range of re- searchers and educators in AI education. Therefore, we will focus on the conceptualization of AI literacy by Long and Magerko (2020), which is among the most frequently cited and established definitions (Laupichler et al., 2022). 

_1.2._ _Current research on AI literacy among students_ 

The current research on AI literacy in higher education focuses on the development and evaluation of specific AI courses (Kandlhofer et al., 2016; Kong et al., 2022; Kong et al., 2021; Lin et al., 2021). To date, only a few research projects have dealt with the measurement of AI literacy. An increasing number of self-assessment scales for AI literacy have been published recently ([Carolus et al., 2023;](#references-table-9) Laupichler et al., 2023; Lin et al., 2023; Ng et al., 2023; Pinski & Benlian, 2023; Wang et al., 2022). However, since self-assessment can be biased (Dunning et al., 2004), a valid and objective knowledge test is needed to assess students’ AI lit- eracy (Laupichler et al., 2023). Some knowledge tests for AI literacy have been developed to evaluate AI courses (Kong et al., 2021, 2022; Wang et al., 2022). Therefore, they often focus on course-specific topics and are thus not suitable for assessing students’ AI literacy in other contexts. As one example, Kong et al. (2021) developed an AI course for students with diverse study backgrounds and showed that course par- ticipants improved in a test about concepts covered in the course. In addition, psychometric measures of these tests are rarely published. Consequently, we set out to develop an AI knowledge test for university students. 

Due to the lack of large-scale surveys, the current state of AI literacy among university students remains mostly unclear. One of the few studies available is a study with healthcare students which reports that the majority of students were unable to define AI or provided an inac- curate definition (Teng et al., 2022). The existing literature on pre- conceptions and misconceptions about AI may inform assumptions about students’ AI literacy. Research suggests that students hold mis- conceptions about AI, such as the idea that AI is very similar to the human brain (Sulmont et al., 2019). In particular, students of non-technical domains have more knowledge gaps regarding AI, as mathematical skills and programming skills were identified as the two biggest barriers to learning about AI (Sulmont et al., 2019). In general, research shows that many learners have a limited technical under- standing of AI ([Antonenko & Abramowitz, 2023;](#references-table-9) Chounta et al., 2022; Evangelista et al., 2018; Lindner & Berges, 2020) and tend to attribute 

human-like characteristics to AI (Evangelista et al., 2018; Kreinsen & Schulz, 2021; Mertala et al., 2022). This research underscores the importance of assessing AI literacy to gain insight into pre-existing knowledge about AI. 

_1.3._ _Rationale_ 

In this study, we aim to develop and validate a theory-based AI lit- eracy test that is compatible with Long and Magerko’s (2020) concep- tualization of AI literacy. Using this test, we assess the AI literacy among university students of different disciplines in Germany, thus contrib- uting to closing the research gap of students’ AI literacy. In addition, we aim to investigate the relationship between AI literacy and other vari- ables, such as students’ prior experience in formal and informal learning opportunities. Considering that AI education programs are beginning to gain wide popularity among instructors, researchers, and in curricula (Su & Zhong, 2022), we expect that most university students in Germany did not learn about AI at school yet (Rietz & Volmicke, 2020¨ ). However, numerous informal learning opportunities are available online (e.g., [https://www.elementsofai.com/)](https://www.elementsofai.com/). Therefore, we expect that AI literacy among university students varies depending on their discipline and in- dividual prior experience in formal or informal learning settings. 

2\. **Method** 

_2.1._ _Test development_ 

_2.1.1._ _Item development_ We generated items theory-driven based on the competencies of Long and Magerko (2020). We decided not to include competency 5 (Imagine Future of AI), as it is not possible to verify predictions, and competencies 14 (Action & Reaction) and 15 (Sensors), because they only focus on one application area of AI (robotics). We used established AI textbooks (Ertel, 2016; Russell & Norvig, 2022) for item generation. Research findings on learners’ misconceptions about AI were used to develop appropriate distractors ([Bewersdorff et al., 2023;](#references-table-9) Lindner & Berges, 2020; Sulmont et al., 2019). We chose a multiple-choice format (one out of four answers is correct) to allow an economic assessment that is suitable for large-scale surveys. This first step resulted in a pool of 57 items. All items were reviewed for technical accuracy and validity by three academic researchers (two computer scientists and one social scientist) in the field of AI. Identified issues (e.g., imprecise use of the terms AI and machine learning) led to revisions. 

_2.1.2._ _Cognitive pretest_ We conducted cognitive interviews with five students from different disciplines (two computer science students, two education students, and one business student). We used the think-aloud method (Willis, 2004) to identify potential hard-to-understand words and misleading phrases. Identified comprehension problems led to revisions of the affected items (e.g., replacing an incomprehensible word with a simpler one). Based on the expert review and cognitive interviews, we excluded less appro- priate, redundant, and interdependent items, resulting in a preliminary number of 39 items. 

_2.1.3._ _Pilot study_ We conducted a subsequent pilot study to obtain descriptive mea- sures of the psychometric quality of the 39 items. For this purpose, we recruited 24 students (11 female, 13 male, age: _M_ = 25.11, _SD_ = 3.23) from different disciplines, e.g., educational sciences, management, psychology, or computer science. Our aim was to include items with a difficulty index between 10% and 90% and a discrimination index be- tween 0.1 and 0.7 (Moosbrugger & Kelava, 2020). The difficulty index represents the proportion of correct responses to each item. We computed a difficulty index that takes into account any potential guessing. The item discrimination index is a measure of how much one 

item correlates with the whole scale. If an item did not meet these the AI literacy test. In IRT, person abilities and item characteristics are criteria, it was revised or excluded. **Attitude.** The relationship between knowledge and attitudes in the field of public understanding of science is well established ([Allum et al., 2008;](#references-table-9) [Bybee & McCrae, 2011)](#references-table-9). Based on these results, we expect AI literacy to correlate positively with positive attitude toward AI and negatively with negative attitude toward AI. We assessed attitude to- ward AI using eight items from the General Attitudes towards AI scale by Schepman and Rodway (2020). We used four items measuring positive attitude (e.g., “There are many beneficial applications of Artificial In- telligence.”) and four items measuring negative attitude (e.g., “I think Artificial Intelligence is dangerous.”). The response format was again a 5-point Likert scale from 1 = strongly disagree to 5 = strongly agree. Internal consistency was acceptable at α = 0.77 for both scales (Tavakol & Dennick, 2011). 

**Discipline and experience with AI.** Students in a technical disci- pline should have a higher level of AI literacy because of prior knowl- edge from courses in their studies (Southworth et al., 2023; Sulmont 

& LMU. 

et al., 2019). Therefore, we assessed the current discipline. Students who use formal and informal learning opportunities should have higher AI literacy than students with little experience with AI. To assess relevant prior experience with AI, students were asked to indicate not only their current discipline but also if they are currently studying computer sci- ence or have studied study computer science in the past. Furthermore, they were asked whether they had ever attended a course on AI. In addition, they were asked to indicate how often they learn about AI in their free time (never/once or twice a year/less than once a month/once or twice a month/once a week/two or three times a week/every day). 

3\. **Results** 

_3.1._ _Descriptive statistics_ 

On average, the participants solved _M_ = 18.79 (_SD_ = 5.57) of the 31 items. Because of the multiple-choice format, it can be expected that, on average, they could have solved 7.75 items by guessing alone. Table 2 shows descriptive statistics of all used AI literacy items. Item difficulty (corrected for guessing) ranged from 0.098 to 0.818. Item

_3.3._ _IRT model selection_ 

As outlined in 2.3, we fitted all three classical IRT models (Rasch, 2- PL, and 3-PL) to the data. We compared multiple model fit and item fit indices to determine which model describes the data best. The model fit indices in Table 3 show that the 3-PL model has a good model fit in all indices, while the Rasch model has an adequate fit only by the RMSEA criterion. The 2-PL model passes the cutoff values for RMSEA and SRMR but closely misses the TLI and CFI criteria. Comparing all three models with each other using AIC and BIC, the 3-PL model describes the data best. 

To evaluate item fit, we used the signed chi-squared (S - Х2) index proposed by Orlando and Thissen (2000). Table 4 presents signed chi-squared item fit indices for all IRT models. Due to multiple testing, 

the _p_-values were corrected for false discovery rate using the method by [Benjamini and Hochberg (1995).](#references-table-9) Compared to the Rasch and the 2-PL model, using the 3-PL model, only a few items do not fit well. Since all model fit and item fit indices support the 3-PL model, we used the 3-PL model for our subsequent analyses. 

_3.4._ _Local independence_ 

AI, and attitude toward AI. Because of the Likert format, we used rating scale models ([Andrich, 1978)](#references-table-9) to calculate IRT person abilities for self-efficacy, interest, positive attitude, and negative attitude (see Table 7 for reliabilities). Table 7 shows the correlations between AI literacy and the affective measures based on IRT scores. As expected, AI literacy correlates significantly positively with self-efficacy, interest, and positive attitude, and significantly negatively with negative attitude. 

_3.7.2._ _Prior experience with AI_ Table 8 shows the prior experience with AI the students reported. Only a minority of students (8.27%) reported studying computer science or having previously studied computer science. About one-fifth (19.59%) have already attended a lecture on AI. The majority (73.47%) learn about AI less frequently than once a month. As outlined previously, we tested whether the AI literacy test can discriminate between students with low and high prior knowledge of AI based on the IRT person ability scores. _3.8._ _Comparison of students’ AI literacy in different disciplines_ 

To compare students’ AI literacy in different disciplines, we only looked at disciplines with at least 30 students to ensure a minimum of statistical interpretability. [Fig. 7 ](#references-table-9)shows the distribution of the IRT score for AI literacy as a function of disciplines. As predicted, students in the field of engineering (including computer science) have the highest AI literacy, followed by other STEM subjects and the social sciences. [Table 9 ](#references-table-9)shows the mean AI literacy IRT score for each discipline. We used post-hoc tests with a family-wise confidence level of 0.95 to determine which differences between disciplines are significant. Only the largest difference between engineering and social sciences is sig- nificant, _p \<_ .001. 

4. **Discussion** 

The aim of this study was to develop and validate an AI literacy test to assess the current state of AI literacy among university students in 

TLI CFI AIC BIC 

We took a theory-based approach to test development, using a well- known competency model for AI literacy (Long & Magerko, 2020). By aligning the test with this widely used definition, we make the test accessible and useable for many researchers and educators. However, other conceptualizations of AI literacy could also serve as a basis for an AI literacy test (Ng et al., 2021). In addition, we contribute to the research gap of an AI literacy test that is not a self-assessment, allowing an objective assessment of knowledge about AI (Laupichler et al., 2023). This complements existing AI literacy tests that rely on self-assessments ([Carolus et al., 2023;](#references-table-9) Laupichler et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2022). We chose a multiple-choice format to allow for economic assessment. A disadvantage is that multiple-choice tasks might not be able to assess a full competency but are rather limited to assessing knowledge. An advantage of our approach is the use of IRT models to analyze the validation data. This allows us to determine the difficulty of each item and to assess the test’s reliability over the whole range of ability (Embretson & Reise, 2009). Our analyses based on IRT show that the test measures in a reliable manner in the middle range of person ability, i.e. the test measures an average level of AI literacy more accurately than a

Due to the validation sample, the AI literacy test presented in this study is suitable for several applications in higher education. This test can be used in screening surveys to assess AI literacy among university students to determine the level of AI literacy in a group or to compare groups. Another possible application could be as an entry diagnostics tool to guide students in choosing an AI course tailored to their prior

In addition, it could be elevated to different use cases like individual assessment or course evaluation.
